A few weeks back I created a brainstorming post seeking ideas and suggestions for improving /v/conspiracy, for making it excellent. There were many neat ideas suggested! I realized that people probably have these sorts of ideas all the time, probably when such posts are not stickied and easy to contribute to, and it would be nice if there were an always-on repository to contribute to. So in similar style to /v/ideasforvoat, I created /v/IdeasForConspiracy to serve as just such a repository.

Anyone may share suggestions or ideas, whether you are a /v/conspiracy regular, new to the community, or standing on the outside looking in, your opinions are welcome and valued here.

My current plans for this subverse are to link this in /v/conspiracymeta, possibly link it in the sidebar of /v/conspiracy, and begin submitting posts about each idea or group of similar ideas shared in the brainstorming discussion and elsewhere, just to sort of seed this initially. Anyone is welcome to post previously shared/discussed ideas as well.

It's true that the content of this subverse may be just as fine on /v/conspiracymeta, and I feel like the non-suggestion content on that subverse may turn off those who just want to have a single, simple place to share, review, and discuss ideas and suggestions themselves, and not deal with other meta-stuff like moderation logs or cross-posts to other day-to-day meta-stuff minutiae. Nothing is stopping ideas from being shared on that subverse or on /v/conspiracy itself, but this one may be more useful for that purpose in terms of aggregation.

Ideas shared here may be those which could only be done by moderators, those which may be done by anyone whether moderator or not, or ideas which might require changes to Voat itself and might be suited for cross-posting to /v/ideasforvoat but have a particular relationship with /v/conspiracy in some way.

Was it true that the Romans lined thier aqua ducts with lead?

Firstly, the use of lead for water pipe construction was widespread in the ancient world. It was malleable, relatively easy to mine, and abundant. In fact, our modern word, plumbing, comes from the Latin word for lead, plumbum. Oddly, the dangers of lead were known, albeit, incompletely, to Greek and Roman physicians because of observed effects on those who mined it. Perhaps due to the fact that the reasons for its danger weren't thoroughly understood or because mineral build-up (Rome seemed to have an abundance of calcium in their water sources) in the lead pipes over time reduced the amount of lead that entered the water and thus the observable harm to people, it was still used by Romans in their plumbing systems but not necessarily ubiquitously. Ceramic pipes were also used. But to drive at your initial question, no. Aqueducts were large scale and traversed the countryside and, to get water from one place to another, were necessarily elevated to create an decline to wherever they terminated. This meant that they were made of stone which, in itself, is a fine means to channel water. That considered, it would have been redundant to line them with lead, as well as making little financial sense. Most of the large scale water infrastructure in Rome was made of stone; aqueducts, cisterns, large scale conduits and channels.

To add to the whole issue of lead use in Rome, there seems to be an disconnect between their understanding that lead could be harmful and they're insistence on using it. For example, lead poisoning was a very real issue in Rome, but it wasn't because of the plumbing. It was because their cookware and utensils were often made of it. Even more startlingly, it was sometime used to sweeten wine. We could only suppose why this inconsistency existed, but it would only be speculation.
